stem: A medical test for a disease is 90% sensitive (correctly identifies a diseased person) and 80% specific (correctly identifies a healthy person). The disease prevalence is 10%. A person tests positive. What is the probability the person actually has the disease?

per_option_rationale.rationale: Returning the test sensitivity P(+|D) = 0.90 as P(D|+), confusing the direction of conditioning.
Computing (sensitivity + prevalence) / 2 = (0.9 + 0.1) / 2 = 0.5, or averaging sensitivity and specificity: (0.9 + 0.8) / 2 = 0.85, then arriving at 0.45 by halving 0.9.
Using only P(D)*P(+|D) = 0.1*0.9 = 0.09 and dividing by P(D) alone (0.1 is not the right denominator), giving 0.09/0.81 = 0.111 via a denominator composition error.

explanation_sections.punchline: A positive test does not mean disease; low prevalence (10%) means most positives are false alarms even with 90% sensitivity.
explanation_sections.approach: Identify model: Bayes theorem with prior = prevalence. Map: P(+|D) = sensitivity = 0.9, P(+|H) = 1 - specificity = 0.2, P(D) = 0.1, P(H) = 0.9. Compute P(+) = 0.9*0.1 + 0.2*0.9 = 0.09 + 0.18 = 0.27. P(D|+) = 0.09/0.27 = 1/3.
explanation_sections.lesson: False-positive rate (1 - specificity) drives down positive predictive value when prevalence is low; never equate sensitivity with the positive predictive value.
explanation_sections.timing: 90 seconds. Three multiplications and one division. The unavoidable trap is returning sensitivity (0.9) as the answer; the correct answer is only 1/3.
